sources.quote: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nijakъ (“neither, none”). By surface analysis, univerbation of ні (ni) + яки́й (jakýj). Compare Russian никако́й (nikakój), Belarusian нія́кі (nijáki), Polish nijaki. Parsable as ні- (ni-) + який (jakyj).

sources.quote: Inherited from Old East Slavic короваи (korovai), from Proto-Slavic *korvajь. Cognate with Russian карава́й (karaváj), Bulgarian крава́й (kraváj), Serbo-Croatian кра̀ва̄ј (“type of cake fed to the bride and groom”) (genitive крава́ја), Slovene kravȃj, krávaj. Per Vasmer, probably related to коро́ва…
sources.note: Wiktionary (en), CC BY-SA 4.0, автори статті — на сторінці; витяг Wiktextract/kaikki.org 2026-10-03

коровай.text: Inherited from Old East Slavic короваи (korovai), from Proto-Slavic *korvajь. Cognate with Russian карава́й (karaváj), Bulgarian крава́й (kraváj), Serbo-Croatian кра̀ва̄ј (“type of cake fed to the bride and groom”) (genitive крава́ја), Slovene kravȃj, krávaj. Per Vasmer, probably related to коро́ва (koróva, “cow, also dialectally bride”); originally thought to have been a wedding gift that was intended to induce fertility.
